title: Networks of identical two-connection nodes can form arrays of any dimension

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Networks of identical two-connection nodes can form arrays of any dimension

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Networks in which every node is identical and has exactly two outgoing connections can, purely by the pattern of connections, form structures equivalent to arrays of any number of dimensions, as well as trees and nested structures.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: using the same principles an array with any number of dimensions can easily be obtained.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 5, “Two Dimensions and Beyond”; section “Network Systems” (from p. 193), p. 196. Scope: directed networks with out-degree two

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch05-09: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.97

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: This is a constructive graph-theoretic existence claim and can be settled by explicit finite-description constructions for arbitrary dimension. No empirical coverage problem remains once the intended notion of equivalence is stated.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For each finite dimension d, encode the integer lattice using vertices with two labeled outgoing edges and a graph construction that represents the required coordinate moves, then exhibit analogous constructions for trees and nested graphs. Verify graph isomorphism to the target structures or identify a degree constraint that makes the construction impossible.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Equivalent to an array depends on whether edges may encode paths rather than immediate neighbors.

Two outgoing connections may need labels or directed-path gadgets.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 1.0
discriminating power: 0.98
operationalizability: 0.92
data adequacy: 0.95
analysis feasibility: 0.98

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Wolfram gives explicit out-degree-two wirings for one, two, and three dimensions and says the same scheme extends. That extension is a short constructive argument: encode an n-dimensional lattice by a fixed local rewiring of identical nodes. Software can verify the small cases, and the inductive construction covers every finite dimension, which is the scope of the claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Exhibit directed graphs in which every node has out-degree two and the connection pattern is that of a line, a square grid, a cubic lattice, a regular tree, or a nested hierarchy, and give the inductive step that raises the dimension by one. A dimension for which no such out-degree-two encoding exists would refute the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Whether a finite graph 'forms' an infinite array or tree is a claim about a repeating connection rule, and the check has to be on that rule rather than on a drawing.

Different layouts of the same graph look different, so the test has to use the connection pattern, not the picture.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.85
discriminating power: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.85
data existence: 0.75
operationalizability: 0.9

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Directed networks in which every node is of one type and has exactly two outgoing connections can realize, through the connection pattern alone, structures equivalent to d-dimensional arrays for every d, as well as trees and nested (fractal) structures. 'Equivalent to a d-dimensional array' is taken in Wolfram's two senses: (i) grouping nodes into identical blocks yields exactly the d-dimensional grid (each block connected to its 2d neighbouring blocks), and (ii) the number of nodes reachable within r connection steps grows like r^d (the network dimension criterion of NKS chapter 9).

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py builds the d-dimensional block network from the single rule in the pre-registration for d = 1..6 and checks, on the torus (Z_5)^d, that every node has two outgoing connections and that contracting blocks gives exactly the grid's edge multiset with 2d distinct neighbouring blocks per block. It runs a breadth-first search along connections on the infinite network from node (0,0) and computes the growth exponent log2(N(R)/N(R/2)) at R = 20 d (d <= 4) or 8 d (d = 5, 6), alongside the same exponent for the plain L1 lattice ball at radius R/d as a finite-size reference. It checks N(r) for the infinite binary tree and constructs the level-7 Sierpinski gasket graph (3282 nodes), orients its 6561 edges along an Euler circuit (Hierholzer) and adds a directed 3-cycle through the corners so that every node has out-degree 2, then measures the growth exponent from a corner (undirected and directed).

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. (1) Arrays: for d = 1..6 construct the network by one uniform rule: each lattice point x of Z^d is a block of d nodes (x, i), i = 0..d-1, and node (x, i) has exactly two outgoing connections, to (x + e_i, (i+1) mod d) and (x - e_i, (i+1) mod d). Verify (a) every node has out-degree exactly 2 and the rule is identical for every node; (b) exact structural equivalence: on the torus (Z_L)^d with L = 5, contracting each block to a point gives a multigraph whose edge set equals the d-dimensional grid's edge set {x <-> x +- e_i} with every block connected to exactly 2d distinct neighbouring blocks (exact set comparison); (c) dimension criterion: breadth-first search along connections from one node of the infinite network, counting N(r) = nodes within r steps; the growth exponent log2(N(R)/N(R/2)) at R = 20 d must lie within 0.5 of d for d = 1, 2, 3, 4 (so that it rounds to d), and is reported (not scored) for d = 5, 6. (2) Trees: the infinite binary tree (node k connects to 2k+1 and 2k+2) has N(r) = 2^(r+1) - 1 for r <= 15 (exact). (3) Nested: the level-7 Sierpinski gasket graph (3 corner nodes of degree 2, all others of degree 4) is given an Eulerian orientation along an Euler circuit plus a directed 3-cycle through the corners, which must give every node out-degree exactly 2; its undirected growth exponent log2(N(R)/N(R/2)) at R = 64 from a corner must lie within 0.3 of log2(3) = 1.585, the gasket's dimension. 'Supports' if (1a), (1b), (1c), (2) and (3) all hold.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if the uniform construction fails structurally for some d <= 6 (out-degree not 2, or the block quotient is not the d-dimensional grid), or if the measured growth exponent for some d <= 4 rounds to an integer other than d, or if no out-degree-2 orientation of the gasket exists. 'Mixed' if arrays pass but the tree or nested construction fails its criterion. 'Inconclusive' is not expected: the test is a self-contained computation.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: growth exponent log2(N(R)/N(R/2)) of the out-degree-2 block network for d = 1..6 (pre-registered window: within 0.5 of d for d <= 4)

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: exact counts; the exponent is biased below d at finite radius exactly as the plain lattice ball is (reference values given)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: The claim is constructive and existential: one explicit family of networks suffices for each d, plus one tree and one nested example. The block-quotient check is the exact sense of 'equivalent to an array'; the growth exponent is Wolfram's own operational notion of network dimension (NKS p. 479 and notes) and adds a check that the effective geometry is d-dimensional without reference to the blocks. Blocks of d nodes connected to 2d neighbouring blocks follow the description on NKS p. 195 ('every block of nodes is connected to four rather than two neighboring blocks'). Growth exponents at finite radius are biased low (the lattice ball itself has local exponent below d at radius ~20), hence the +-0.5 window; the exact quotient check is the decisive part.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Out-degree-2 networks generated by analysis.py

NKS pp. 195-196, 'Network Systems' (online edition)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Deviation from the pre-registration: for d = 5 and 6 (reported, not scored) the BFS radius was reduced from 20d to 8d because the 20d search for d = 6 visited 13 million nodes (68 s and several GB in a first run; it gave exponent 5.756 and the d = 5 run at radius 50 gave 4.815). At radius 8d the exponents are 4.74 and 5.65, still rounding to d and above the plain lattice ball's finite-radius exponents (4.26 and 4.96), so the conclusion is unchanged.

The claim is existential and is settled by the exact quotient check for d <= 6 together with the uniform rule, which is defined for every d (the same code runs for any d; only the search radius limits the computation). The growth-exponent check is Wolfram's operational notion of dimension and confirms the effective geometry without using the block structure; its finite-radius bias is quantified by the lattice reference.

One construction per structure type is tested (block arrays; binary tree; Eulerian-oriented Sierpinski gasket). The gasket orientation plus corner 3-cycle is one way to get out-degree exactly 2 for every node; the undirected growth exponent 1.612 and directed 1.594 are both within 0.03 of log2(3), the gasket's Hausdorff dimension.

Whether the resulting networks are 'equivalent' to arrays in any stronger sense (e.g. as substrates for network cellular automata, NKS p. 1031) was not tested; the block-quotient isomorphism and dimension are the two senses stated in the pre-registration.
